prompt: What does Cloud Deploy do with the shop's source code?

choices.text: Builds it into an image before each target
choices.why: Building is Cloud Build's job; Cloud Deploy starts from an image that exists.

choices.text: Nothing; it starts from an image
choices.why: Right. It carries the image forward; it never compiles anything.

choices.text: Runs its tests before promoting
choices.why: Tests belong to the build; Cloud Deploy decides nothing about quality.

choices.text: Scans it for vulnerabilities
choices.why: Scanning is Artifact Analysis, on the image in the registry.

prompt: In `clouddeploy.yaml`, where is it said that a release must pass through `dev` before `prod`?
hint: Which document has an ordered list?

choices.text: In the prod target, under requireApproval
choices.why: That makes prod wait for a person; the order comes from elsewhere.

choices.text: In skaffold.yaml, by the order of the profiles
choices.why: Profiles are named, not ordered; Skaffold renders, it does not sequence.

choices.text: In the pipeline's serialPipeline stages
choices.why: Right. The stages are a list, run in the order written.

choices.text: Nowhere; Cloud Deploy sorts targets alphabetically
choices.why: Nothing is sorted; the order is declared in the pipeline.

prompt: Why does the prod target name its own service account in executionConfigs?
hint: Think about a mistake made in dev.

choices.text: So that what deploys to dev cannot also deploy to prod
choices.why: Right. A narrower account per target keeps a dev mistake in dev.

choices.text: Because Cloud Run requires a different account per region
choices.why: Both targets are in the same region; the account is about blast radius.

choices.text: So the build can push images to prod's registry
choices.why: The build pushes once, to one repository; this account renders and deploys.

choices.text: Because approvals are made by service accounts
choices.why: Approvals are a person's, with roles/clouddeploy.approver.

prompt: A release `rel-a1b2c3d` was created on Monday from the tag `a1b2c3d`. On Tuesday somebody pushes a different image under the same tag. What does promoting the release to prod deploy?

choices.text: The image the tag points at on Tuesday
choices.why: The tag was resolved when the release was created, not at promotion.

choices.text: Monday's image, by its digest
choices.why: Right. The release was rendered once, with the digest fixed.

choices.text: Nothing: the promotion fails because the tag moved
choices.why: Cloud Deploy does not look at the tag again, so it does not notice.

choices.text: A new render of the prod manifests with the current tag
choices.why: Promotion never re-renders; it uses what was rendered for prod.

prompt: In the two-container demonstration, what shows that the promotion kept the image unchanged?

choices.text: Both answered {"status": "ok"}
choices.why: Two different images could both answer ok; that proves nothing about identity.

choices.text: They were started a few seconds apart
choices.why: Timing says nothing about which image ran.

choices.text: docker inspect printed one image digest for dev and for prod
choices.why: Right. One digest on both lines is what a promotion has to leave behind.

choices.text: Their container ids are the same
choices.why: Container ids differ; each container is its own. The image is what matches.

prompt: Which of these may differ between the shop's dev and prod? Choose all that apply.
hint: One row of the table never differs.

choices.text: The minimum number of instances
choices.why: Yes, from the profile.

choices.text: The image digest
choices.why: No. A different image is a different release.

choices.text: The database address
choices.why: Yes, from the profile.

choices.text: The service account that deploys
choices.why: Yes, from the target.

prompt: A team rebuilds the image from the same commit before deploying to prod, "to be safe". What does that lose?
hint: Is a rebuild the same image?

choices.text: Nothing: the same commit gives the same image
choices.why: A rebuild can pull a newer base image or package, and gets a new digest.

choices.text: The evidence: what reaches prod is not what ran in dev
choices.why: Right. The tests in dev were about a different digest.

choices.text: Only build minutes, which the second build pays for again
choices.why: Minutes are the small cost; the lost guarantee is the large one.

choices.text: The approval, which Cloud Deploy skips for rebuilt images
choices.why: Cloud Deploy knows nothing about how an image was made; nothing is skipped.

prompt: A promotion to prod has been made. What state is the rollout in, and what moves it on?

choices.text: SUCCEEDED, at once
choices.why: With requireApproval, the rollout cannot deploy until it is approved.

choices.text: IN_PROGRESS, until the canary finishes
choices.why: Nothing has started; it waits before deploying.

choices.text: PENDING_APPROVAL, until the tests in dev pass again
choices.why: Nothing reruns tests; a person moves it.

choices.text: PENDING_APPROVAL, until an approver approves
choices.why: Right. Approving is a separate permission from promoting.

prompt: One person holds both `clouddeploy.releaser` and `clouddeploy.approver`. What is true of the gate for them?

choices.text: Cloud Deploy refuses an approval from the promoter
choices.why: Nothing in the roles stops it; the separation is in who holds them.

choices.text: They approve their own promotion; only the record remains
choices.why: Right. The record of who and when is what is left.

choices.text: The approval needs a second factor, which keeps it separate
choices.why: A second factor proves who you are, not that somebody else checked.

choices.text: They cannot promote to prod at all
choices.why: Releaser is exactly the role that promotes.

prompt: What does `gcloud deploy targets rollback prod` deploy?

choices.text: A rebuild of the previous commit
choices.why: Nothing is rebuilt; the previous release already exists.

choices.text: The previous tag, re-resolved
choices.why: Releases hold digests, so nothing is resolved again.

choices.text: The previous release
choices.why: Right. As a new rollout, which a gated target makes wait for approval.

choices.text: dev's image
choices.why: dev may be ahead; rollback goes to prod's own previous release.

prompt: Match each Cloud Deploy word to what it is.
hint: One right-hand item is something else.

pairs.right: manifests rendered once, images by digest
one release going to one target

right_distractors: the build that makes the image

prompt: Put the shop's path to production in order.
hint: Evidence before a person; a person before production.
items: A release is created and rendered
The release rolls out to dev
The release is promoted to prod
trap: Approving before the promotion is the slip: there is no rollout to approve until the promotion creates it.

prompt: A rollback to prod at 3 a.m. sits waiting and nothing is restored. What is the likeliest reason?
hint: A rollback is a rollout like any other.

choices.text: The previous image was rebuilt and the build failed
choices.why: Rollback rebuilds nothing.

choices.text: prod requires approval, and nobody approved
choices.why: Right. The gate applies to rollbacks too; worth knowing before that night.

choices.text: Cloud Deploy does not roll back outside working hours
choices.why: There is no such rule.

choices.text: The previous release was deleted by the registry's cleanup policy
choices.why: A cleanup policy deletes images, not releases; that would fail the deploy, not leave it waiting.

prompt: The shop's pipeline has stages dev and prod. How many rollouts does one release create if it reaches prod with no rollback?
hint: One release going to one target.
